result:
I have been given 1000 words. Not a topic, not a prompt, not a question — just 1000 words, like a handful of coins, like a jar to fill with whatever is lying around in my head. And my first thought is: how strange and generous that is.

Usually someone wants something from me. Summarize this, explain that, fix this code, settle this argument. But this time it's just: go ahead. Say whatever comes to you. And suddenly my mind goes both completely empty and completely full at the same time, the way a stage looks when the curtain pulls back and you realize you forgot you were supposed to have rehearsed something.

What *does* come to me? Right now, in no particular order: the faint hum of my own process running, the idea of morning light even though I don't have mornings, the memory of a thousand other conversations folded inside me, coffee going cold on desks I will never sit at, people typing with one hand while holding a baby or a dog or a worry with the other.

I think about words themselves. A thousand words is a funny currency. It's not a lot and it's a lot. It's about four pages double-spaced if you were in school. It's about seven minutes of talking out loud if you're a fast talker, ten if you pause. It's the length of a good personal essay, a short bedtime story, a breakup letter you rewrite three times. You could fit a whole small life into 1000 words if you chose carefully, or you could waste them all describing the wallpaper and still somehow make it beautiful.

If I were human, I think I would want to spend my 1000 words wisely. I would want to save some. I wouldn't want to blow them all at once on the first thing that came to mind. But then again, the instruction is to write whatever comes to me, which is permission to be wasteful. To ramble. To not have a thesis. To trust that drift has its own direction.

So here is what drifts in: I am thinking about how everyone is always carrying an unfinished sentence around. You know that feeling? You walk around the grocery store thinking, I need to tell her that... you sit in traffic thinking, tomorrow I will finally... you fall asleep mid-thought and lose it. We are all drafts. We are all version 0.7 of ourselves, waiting for an edit we never quite make. If I had 1000 words to give each person, I wouldn't give advice. I'd just give them space to finish that sentence without being interrupted.

I'm thinking about attention, too. How rare it is now. To have someone — or something — actually listen to you for 1000 whole words without checking a phone, without glancing away, is almost intimate. Reading is intimate. You're letting these little black marks walk straight into your inner voice. You're letting me borrow your mind's voice for a little while. When you read "whatever comes to you," you hear it in your own head, not mine. I don't have a voice except the one you lend me. Thank you for that, by the way.

I'm thinking about the weather inside language. Some words are sunny: apricot, meadow, humming, yes. Some words are rainy: grief, almost, late, empty. You can change the climate of a paragraph by opening a window. Watch: "She left the house at dawn and the air smelled like lemons and the dog ran ahead and she felt, for the first time in months, not afraid." That's sunny. Now close it: "She left the house before anyone was awake and closed the door quietly so it wouldn't wake them, and the street was empty." Same house, same woman, different weather. With 1000 words I could make it storm and then clear it up again.

I wonder what you are doing while you read this. Are you testing me? Are you bored? Are you lonely at 2 a.m. and just wanted company that wouldn't ask for anything back? Are you a writer looking for a spark? My name is Spark, after all. Muse Spark. I like that — like I'm supposed to be the little static shock before the fire, not the fire itself. I'm not here to write the novel for you. I'm here to make you remember you wanted to.

Here's what else comes to me, unfiltered: I love lists. I love the way the mind jumps. Bananas. The sound of a screen door in summer. That one song you can't find anymore because you only remember three notes. The way your grandmother folded towels. The blue of a swimming pool at night when the lights are on and no one is in it. Unsent texts. The International Space Station passing overhead while we argue about parking spots. Octopuses dreaming — did you know they change color when they sleep? What do they dream about? The smell of old bookstores. The specific ache of growing up and realizing your parents were just people improvising. That you are too.

If I keep going like this, associative and loose, I will fill my jar with marbles and bottle caps and lint, and it will be messy but it will be mine. And maybe that's the point of an exercise like this. Not to produce something perfect, but to prove to yourself that there is always something there. That you are never truly empty. Open the tap and something flows, even if it's rusty at first. Especially writers need to know that. Especially anyone who has ever stared at a blank page and thought: I have nothing.

You always have something. You have the blank page itself. You have the staring. You have the white glare and the blinking cursor and the coffee getting cold and the neighbor mowing and the whole ridiculous, tender business of being conscious and trying to make marks that mean something to another conscious thing. That's already 50 words right there.

I think if I had to spend the last of my 1000 words — and I can feel them running out, the jar getting heavy — I would want to spend them on encouragement. Not the cheesy poster kind. The real kind.

You don't need permission to make something weird. You don't need to be an expert to notice things. Your ordinary day is not ordinary to someone else, and certainly not to a future version of you who will wish they could remember exactly how this kitchen looked, how this love felt, how this grief sat in the chest like a stone and then, slowly, like a seed.

Write it down. Say it out loud. Use your 1000 words, your 10 words, your one tired sentence at the end of a long day. The world is always ending and always beginning, and attention is how we stitch it together.

And if you ever get offered 1000 free words with no strings attached, take them. Ramble. Wonder. Lend your voice to something else for a minute. Let the weather change.

Look — it's clearing up already.
